name: Dingo
_note: Numbers are first-pass placeholders, chosen for realism and for the director to tune. Facts and text are drafts, to be checked against sources before release. Dingoes are never villains: hunting is what keeps the ecosystem in balance.

needs.label: Water
needs.issue: Thirsty: no water in its territory

needs.label: Prey
needs.issue: Hungry: not enough prey in its territory for the pack

issue_parts.shelter: No den: no rocky outcrop, empty burrow or (for a small family) hollow log nearby

needs.label: Family
needs.issue: Alone: its family hasn't joined it yet

hunt_facts: Dingoes are Australia's top land predator. By hunting kangaroos, they stop them overgrazing the land.
Most dingo hunts fail. Kangaroos can bound away at over 50 km/h.
Where dingoes hunt, smaller predators like foxes and feral cats are kept in check too, which helps small native animals.
Dingoes often hunt in pairs or family groups, taking turns to tire their prey.
text.hunt_success: The dingo has fed. Hunting keeps kangaroo numbers in balance with the land.
text.hunt_fail: This time the kangaroo got away.

facts: Dingoes have lived in Australia for at least 3,500 years.
Dingoes live in family packs, usually with one breeding pair.
They den in rocky outcrops, hollow logs and old burrows dug by other animals.
Dingoes howl to keep in touch with their pack across their territory, and to warn rival packs away.
A dingo can rotate its wrists, which helps it climb and grip.
Rival dingo packs keep to their own territories, and compete for water, dens and prey.
